title: Inside Out & Back Again (Selected Poems)
author: Thanhha Lai
citation: Lai, Thanhha. Inside Out & Back Again. HarperCollins Children's Books, 2011.

sections.heading: 1975: Year of the Cat & Papaya Tree

epigraph.quote: No one would believe me, but at ten I still feel the urge to step on the tile floor first on Tet, just to see what happens.

paragraphs: Every new year Mother visits the I Ching Teller of Fate. This year he predicts our lives will twist inside out. The war is coming closer to our home in Saigon. The sound of distant bombing echoes like thunder rolling over the horizon, shaking the wooden shutters of our house.

In our backyard grows a papaya tree that I nurtured from a tiny black seed. I love watching the glossy green leaves spread wide like open palms, shading the cluster of young papayas that cling to the trunk like green globes. Every morning I check their growth, measuring how their smooth skins ripen toward golden yellow. To me, the papaya tree represents life, sweetness, and hope in a city surrounded by turmoil.

sections.heading: Saigon is Gone & The Open Sea

epigraph.quote: Commander announces: 'Saigon is gone.' Droves of people drop to the deck and weep.

paragraphs: When the final orders come, Brother Khoi and Mother pack small cloth bundles with essential clothes, family photographs, and a handful of dried rice. We race toward the navy harbor under a sky darkened by smoke and burning fuel depots. Helicopters circle above like agitated hornets, dropping personnel into the South China Sea once their fuel runs out.

We squeeze onto a packed navy barge with hundreds of other families, our shoulders pressed tight against strangers. On the open sea, fresh water is rationed by the sip, and cooked rice is dry and hard. When the ship captain announces over the megaphone that Saigon has fallen to the Northern army, a collective wail rises from the deck. Our country is gone, our home is left behind, and we are floating between who we were and what we must become.

sections.heading: Back Again: Learning English in Alabama

epigraph.quote: I want to explain that in Vietnamese I am smart, funny, and bold. In English, I sound like an infant learning to chew.

paragraphs: In Alabama, everything smells different—of floor wax, cold fried chicken, and sweet tea. At school, the other children stare at my black hair and quiet posture. English words feel heavy and awkward on my tongue; the rules of grammar seem arbitrary, with words that do not sound the way they look.

Yet slowly, with each spelling test mastered, each tentative friendship formed, and the warmth of Mother's encouragement, the feeling of being turned inside out begins to recede. We plant new seeds in Alabama soil. We learn that home is not merely a house on a quiet street in Saigon; home is the courage of a family that remains bound together across oceans and through grief, learning to blossom once again.
